The scroll-world hero is one continuous camera flight scrubbed by scroll — five scenes, CSS 3D rather than video, so it stays crisp and respects reduced-motion.

Hero is the two-door skeleton shared with Toys and 3D Printing: get on the left, give on the right, three live numbers. Handoff: Magic UI NumberTicker + DotPattern, Motion stagger on load, prefers-reduced-motion snaps. The facet panel is sticky so the result count never scrolls out of view.

Five tabs keep a long guide skimmable; Community notes is where builders add the step the author missed, attached to a step and pinnable by the author, backing org or admin as a revision. Pins surface as a strip above Steps and a count on the step, and are appended to the PDF. A note can also be filed against no step at all — the Missing step button beside the step picker — and pinning that renders it as an extra numbered step at the foot of the list, so a builder can supply what the author left out. Thanks is one tap, shown as a count. Report a problem is the same quiet flag everywhere and goes to SPLAT only. The sidebar answers the two questions a parent actually has: how long, and how much.

Same two-door hero as Guides: request on the left, "outgrown it? pass it on" on the right. Every toy here is given, not sold. Condition is a five-star scale because "good" means nothing between strangers.
The public view of one listed toy. Distance, condition and what is actually in the box come before the request button — those are the three facts that decide it.
Where an exchange starts. A swap asks you to pick one of your own listed toys; a donation is a one-way ask the holder accepts or declines. Both send the same note about the child.
Five questions, all skippable, saved locally. The mascot carries the tone so the form never feels like an assessment.
One free course, six units, sixteen lessons. Coursera-style course home (outcomes, outline, progress ring) over a Duolingo-style ordered path; nothing is locked. Progress saves locally for guests.
The whole trick in one paragraph, up front. Everything else is elaboration.
Force and cost are given per switch because those are the two facts that decide it.
Good/walk-away as two columns, then a two-minute in-shop test. Written to be used standing in an aisle.
The borrow column matters more than the cost column — a soldering iron used twice a year is a waste.
Button cells lead, because they are the one non-negotiable. Cleaning and handover moved to their own lesson in Unit 6.
Not a queue. A router: sends each kind of question to the place it already gets answered (community notes, Learn, a public Question, the help sheet). No unmanaged inbox.
A button is a gap in a circuit; the external switch is a second way to close it. Two diagrams carry the whole lesson.
Three questions, instant feedback, wrong answers explain themselves. Nothing is locked behind it.
The one soldering job the whole course rests on. Nine photographed steps, identical for jack and socket.
Three questions on the connector build.
Workshop toy one. Solder to a board.
Workshop toy two. Solder to button legs, plus the strain-relief knot.
Makers Making Change guide (CC BY-SA). A splice, not a board; two sockets for two functions.
Four printed parts and a limit switch. Links to 3D Printing for anyone without a printer.
Five safety checks as cards, cleaning, and the two minutes of showing the family.
Four questions across the course; passing it ends with the mascot and a pointer to the Guides.

The section’s home. Leads with "you do not need a printer", then the same rail as Guides and Toys. Pick up to three printers; the first to accept wins and the rest withdraw themselves. Guests see the list dimmed behind the unlock card.
Written to be handed to whoever owns the printer, so settings come before philosophy.
Parts come from the guide, never uploaded. Tick any combination, one request. The printer sees your suburb and your note, nothing else.
Three audience doors, then concrete small actions. Nobody self-identifies as a "contributor" until they see the path.
Ends by offering the toy library, because building is not for everyone right now.
Step 1 is photograph as you go — the failure mode nobody warns about.
Leadership is granted by an admin, never self-started. That is the trust model.

Signed-in only, since we need to know who to verify. Identity, what the org does, and how to check the requester actually works there — an admin reviews every one before an organisation or a leader is created.
Anonymity is offered because the best ideas come from people who feel unqualified to post.
Explains review before asking for work, so a rejection is never a surprise.
Build requests tied to an existing guide. A parent asks, a maker nearby claims, and the rest is an ordinary exchange.
Mirrors /toys/[id]/request: pick the guide, say who it is for, agree how far you can travel. The note is the only free text.
The exchange thread with one extra stage: the maker posts a working shot and the family approves it before handover.
Open problems as cards. Maker and post counts signal whether a challenge is alive.
Brief, constraints, then thread. A solved challenge graduates into a guide rather than closing.
Three charts only: delivery over time, guides by difficulty, deliveries by state. Anything more is decoration.
Search plus three filters. "Has a printer" is the one people actually use.

Answers a family’s five questions in order: what do they do, how do I use it, what have they backed, who are they, where and when. Printer card gives machines, materials and turnaround because that is what a requester compares. Follow and Message gate on sign-in. Backed guides come before held toys — the endorsement is the organisation’s real contribution.

LinkedIn header (cover, avatar, headline, one primary action), GitHub-style build heatmap, Printables-style earned badges, and a thanks wall in place of a follower count. Work first: a pinned Featured guide, then the grid with filters.
Date-grouped list with a date badge, host and one-tap RSVP (Luma/Meetup pattern). Format and state filters; online events show in every state. Past events fold away.
Leads with the four things a family decides on: what, when, where, who it is for. RSVP, add-to-calendar (.ics), host card. Online links are never public.

The RSVP is a form, not a toggle: name and email always, then whatever the organiser added when they published the event. Required answers block the confirm; everything else is optional by default. Answers land on the leader’s manage page.

Waste plastic in, filament out. Organisations publish what their machines can actually take; contributors book a drop-off, declare its condition, and the organisation issues print credit only after it weighs it at the door. Two-kilo minimum so a machine run is worth firing up.
Pick the organisation, say what and how much, then tick every line of the condition declaration. The estimate is honest about yield — about three quarters of what you bring becomes filament.
Two halves: what your machines can take, and the queue of booked drop-offs. Credit is minted here, by weighing — never by the contributor.
One featured story, then a filterable grid by story type. Every story is attributed to an organisation and a byline.
Reading column at 68ch, one pull quote, one link back into the product (guide, profile, org).
Three pillars: no paid tier, reviewed not just posted, information not devices. The third is a regulatory position.
Everyone here does something else for a living, and the bios say so.
Topic chips route the message. Safety reports jump the queue and the page says so.
Every ask a family can make of an organisation, in one queue: host a build day, print parts for an event, build a guide nearby. Accept, decline or hand on.
RSVPs with the part-print status per event. A declined print shows the next step, not just the word.
Contact-form messages by topic. Safety jumps the queue; everything else is oldest first.
Makers-wanted oversight: unclaimed for two weeks, claimed but silent for ten days. Nudge or reopen.
Leader side of the help pipeline: accept or decline part-print requests from families, see who is coming.
Grouped by role, not dollar tier: delivery partners (live from the org list), funders with what each grant paid for, in-kind partners, one quote, past supporters last.
Non-money asks first (skills, parts, organisations, ideas), a workplace build day, then funding. Not DGR yet, so it says so and routes funders to a conversation.
The only policy page written to be read by a tired parent rather than a lawyer.
Child profiles are readable only by the owning account, enforced at the database rather than in app code.
Opens by stating the platform is free and always will be.
Assumes good faith and short time — most gaps are someone running out of evening.
Draws the line between describing an adaptation and making a device claim.
You keep the copyright; we keep it available so a half-finished build does not lose its instructions.
Backing a guide means a competent person read it. That claim is the whole risk.
One hub, twelve doors, badge counts on anything waiting. Replaces the old sidebar entirely.
Status is the primary sort: a returned guide should be the first thing you see.
Asks for two things only. Everything else waits for the editor.

Every field the reader sees has an input here: guide kind (which decides whether a Files tab exists), cover photo, works-with, per-step title, minutes and watch-out note, structured parts with cost, print settings, and the three "worth a look" picks. Seven sections, each independently saveable, with a completeness note. Nothing is public until submitted.
Given-away toys stay visible but dimmed — people want the record.
Condition is four plain-language grades (Like new, Good, Well-loved, Needs a fix) — a description of the object, not a score, so it cannot be mistaken for a rating of the giver.
Requests are answered inline. Accept/decline never needs a second screen.
"Waiting on you" is a first-class state, surfaced as a chip on the row.
System events sit centred between messages so the record reads chronologically.
The interactive version: type and send, then confirm the handoff. Both sides must confirm.
A rejected idea keeps the reviewer’s reason attached, visible only to its author.
Split into what is savable today and what is planned, so the empty categories are honest.
Unread rows carry a tinted background as well as a dot — colour alone is not a signal.
Status is the sort. Anything waiting on you — a code to enter, a fit to confirm — rises to the top.
One status rail, one thread. Pickup details appear only at Ready, copied from the printer’s profile the moment they accepted — same rule as toy exchanges.
Three tabs: printers, requests, jobs. Declining needs a reason, marking ready needs a photo. Live in the prototype — accept here and the requester’s job page moves.
Bed size and materials decide which requests you are offered. Availability is a toggle plus a capacity number; either one closes you.
Email is frozen; capabilities are shown as chips so a leader can see what they hold.
Every field optional, private to the account, and phrased around a bad day rather than a best one.
Blocked until the leader terms are accepted — read access, no approve.

Every field on the public organisation page has an input here: identity, the About paragraph, which capabilities show as chips, the three doors, the declared rates families are quoted, and how a family reaches you. No review — it publishes on save, so the leader terms are restated at the foot.
Needs-cleaning is a status, because it is the one that stalls a handoff.
What the organisation has published, in two tabs. Publish/unpublish is one click and takes effect on the public page immediately — no review, so the leader terms are restated at the foot.
Four required things (name, date+time, where, who for). Online events hide the link until RSVP. Publish goes straight to the public page; Save as draft goes to the list.
Type, title, one-sentence summary, body with live word count, byline. Publish is disabled until consent is confirmed for everyone named or pictured.

The same three tabs as Print for others, scoped to the organisation’s machines. A request is accepted ONTO a machine: the card fit-checks each bench (material loaded, free slot, bed size) and preselects the best one; a leader can override. The chosen machine is stamped on the job so other leaders know which bench it is on. Pickup point is the org’s and cannot be varied.

The pages nobody else owns: home hero and headline numbers, the team and partner lists, the Learn course outline, and the four legal documents with their version and effective date. Legal edits can force re-acceptance, so that is a deliberate toggle rather than a side effect.
Five queues, each a number waiting for a person. Nothing else on the page.
Master-detail with a drawer: approve or send back without losing your place in the queue.
Section-by-section verdicts plus a checklist. A rejection reason must be specific enough to act on.
Private problem reports. Safety sorts to the top regardless of age. Each has three states and a note back to the reporter; the reported person is never shown who filed it.
Publishing turns an idea into a public brief with a thread; rejecting keeps it private to its author.
Every job on the platform. Stalled — accepted but not moved in ten days — is a status of its own and sorts to the top.
Audits what org leaders approved. Repeated bad approvals suspend the organisation.
Side drawer for leaders and the danger zone. Suspension keeps guides live but blocks new approvals.
Flagged rows are tinted and sorted up.
Explains the terms gate before asking for a password.
Returns you to whatever you were saving when you were interrupted.
Scrollable, accepted once, versioned. Blocks first submission, not browsing.
The Soft Pop kit: ramp, elevation, the bear mascot in five poses and every component in one place.
Default, hover, focus, active, disabled and loading for each control class.
